about: Ten ideas from Taschner's script for TU Wien's Mathematik 1 and 2 for electrical engineering (Taschner_Skr_mathe1-2.pdf, 505 pages, no title page, date or table of contents; it ends with Cauchy's integral theorem). Its text layer is scrambled, so every formula was read from the rendered pages on 2 Nov 2026 and is cited by printed page: printed page = PDF page up to p. 360 or so, PDF page − 12 near the end (p. 400 is PDF 412, p. 493 is PDF 505). The script has no exercises; practice answers are its own worked values where it gives them, otherwise worked by hand, and each says which. Laplace transforms and linear differential equations are in the Automation Lab, Fourier series in the Signals and Systems Lab.

labs.title: The Babylonian square root
labs.idea: A rectangle of area a is made squarer by replacing its sides x and a/x by their mean. Step by step its side homes in on √a, the number of right digits about doubling each time.

equations.note: the first step for a = 10 from x = 3: the mean of the sides 3 and 10/3
the new side is a little too long
the second step; (721/228)² = 10 + 1/51984

practice.question: Start the Babylonian method for a = 10 at x = 3. What is the side after two steps?

labs.title: Complex numbers: turn and stretch
labs.idea: Multiplying by a complex number z = r(cos φ + j sin φ) stretches by its modulus r and turns by its argument φ. So moduli multiply and arguments add, and powers turn round the circle.
labs.law: |zζ| = |z|·|ζ|,  arg zζ = arg z + arg ζ

equations.eq: z = r (cos φ + j sin φ)
equations.note: the polar form, with the modulus r = |z| and the argument φ = arg z

equations.eq: |zζ| = |z|·|ζ|,  arg zζ = arg z + arg ζ
equations.note: Gauss's geometric reading of the product: a turn and a stretch
the same product in components

equations.eq: (cos φ + j sin φ)ⁿ = cos nφ + j sin nφ
equations.note: de Moivre's formula

practice.question: z has modulus 1 and argument 50°. What is the argument of z⁸, between 0° and 360°?
practice.source: Worked by hand from de Moivre's formula, Taschner p. 94

labs.title: The geometric series
labs.idea: Adding 1 + q + q² + … term by term closes in on 1/(1 − q), but only when |q| < 1. Otherwise the same neat formula gives nonsense, which is why limits are needed.

equations.tex: s = 1 + q + q^2 + \dots, \quad qs = s - 1 \;\Rightarrow\; s = \frac{1}{1 - q}
equations.note: Leibniz's trick, which only holds when the series has a sum
the trick applied to q = 2: the script's warning

practice.question: What is 1 + 0.6 + 0.6² + 0.6³ + …?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Taschner p. 126

labs.title: The integral as an area
labs.idea: Cover the area under a curve with bars as high as the least value on each part (the lower sum) and as high as the greatest (the upper sum). The area lies between the two, and finer parts squeeze them together.
labs.law: Σ p_m (x_m − x_{m−1}) ≤ ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx ≤ Σ q_m (x_m − x_{m−1})

equations.eq: Σ q_m (x_m − x_{m−1}), with p_m ≤ f(x) ≤ q_m on [x_{m−1}; x_m]
equations.tex: \sum_{m=1}^{n} q_m (x_m - x_{m-1}), \qquad p_m \le f(x) \le q_m \text{ on } [x_{m-1}; x_m]
equations.note: the upper sum (Obersumme); with p_m the lower sum (Untersumme)
the area, at least the lower and at most the upper sum, after Riemann

practice.question: Split [0, 1] into 10 equal parts. What is the upper sum of f(x) = x²?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Taschner p. 166

labs.title: From secant to tangent
labs.idea: The secant through two points of a curve cuts it twice. Slide the second point onto the first and the secant turns into the tangent, which only touches; its slope is the differential quotient dy/dx.

equations.tex: \Delta X = \begin{pmatrix} \Delta x \\ \Delta y \end{pmatrix} \;\to\; dX = \begin{pmatrix} dx \\ dy \end{pmatrix}
equations.note: the secant's direction ΔX becomes the tangent's dX; between them Leibniz's characteristic triangle

equations.eq: k = dy/dx = −x/y on the circle x² + y² = r²
equations.note: the script's example: the tangent's slope on a circle

practice.question: For f(x) = x³ − 2x, what is the slope of the secant from x = 0.6 to x = 0.61?

labs.title: Newton's method
labs.idea: Follow the tangent at a guess down to the x-axis: where it lands is a better guess. Near a root the error roughly squares with every step.

equations.note: the slope triangle of the tangent
Newton's formula (Newtonformel)
for n-th roots; n = 2 is the Babylonian method

practice.question: Newton's formula for f(x) = x³ − 2, started at x = 1: what is the guess after two steps?

labs.title: Pointwise, not uniform
labs.idea: Bumps that grow narrower and taller, each of area 1, go to zero at every point except 0. Yet their integrals stay 1: without uniform convergence the limit and the integral may not be swapped.
labs.law: lim n→∞ φₙ(t) = 0 for t ≠ 0,  but  ∫ φₙ(t) dt = 1

equations.eq: φₙ(t) = cₙ e^(−n²/(1 − n²t²)) for |t| < 1/n, else 0
equations.tex: \varphi_n(t) = c_n\, e^{-n^2/(1 - n^2 t^2)} \text{ for } |t| < 1/n, \quad 0 \text{ otherwise}
equations.note: the bump, smooth and zero outside ]−1/n; 1/n[; cₙ makes its integral 1

equations.eq: |fₙ(x) − f(x)| < ε for all n ≥ n₀, n₀ independent of x
equations.tex: |f_n(x) - f(x)| < \varepsilon \text{ for all } n \ge n_0, \; n_0 \text{ independent of } x
equations.note: uniform convergence; pointwise, n₀ may depend on x

equations.eq: ∫ₐᵇ lim fₙ dx = lim ∫ₐᵇ fₙ dx  when fₙ → f uniformly
equations.note: the swap that uniform convergence allows

practice.question: How high is the bump φ₂ at t = 0?
practice.solution: φ₂(0) = c₂ e^(−4), with c₂ from ∫ φ₂ = 1; the script gives the maximum 2.605…, against 0.828… for φ₁ and 9.424… for φ₄.

labs.title: Two equations, two lines
labs.idea: Each linear equation in x and y is a line. Two lines meet in one point exactly when the determinant is not zero; then Cramer's rule gives the point as quotients of determinants.
labs.law: x = det(b, a₂)/det(a₁, a₂),  y = det(a₁, b)/det(a₁, a₂)
labs.lawTex: x = \frac{\begin{vmatrix} b_1 & a_{12} \\ b_2 & a_{22} \end{vmatrix}}{\begin{vmatrix} a_{11} & a_{12} \\ a_{21} & a_{22} \end{vmatrix}}, \qquad y = \frac{\begin{vmatrix} a_{11} & b_1 \\ a_{21} & b_2 \end{vmatrix}}{\begin{vmatrix} a_{11} & a_{12} \\ a_{21} & a_{22} \end{vmatrix}}

equations.note: the two-row determinant, the sum over the two orders of 1, 2 with their signs

equations.eq: x_m = vol(…, u_{m−1}, w, u_{m+1}, …)/vol(u₁, u₂, …, u_n)
equations.tex: x_m = \frac{\operatorname{vol}(\dots, u_{m-1}, w, u_{m+1}, \dots)}{\operatorname{vol}(u_1, u_2, \dots, u_n)}
equations.note: Cramer's rule: replace the m-th column by the right-hand side

practice.question: Solve 2x + y = 5, x + 3y = 10. What is x?
practice.source: Worked by hand with Cramer's rule, Taschner p. 400

labs.title: Eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix
labs.idea: A symmetric matrix turns the unit circle into an ellipse. Along two directions at right angles, the eigenvectors, it does not turn at all, only stretches, by the eigenvalues.

equations.eq: Q(φ) = a cos²φ + 2b sin φ cos φ + c sin²φ
equations.note: the quadratic form on the unit vectors
the stationary directions
the eigenvalues, with the eigenvectors u = cos φ₀ + j sin φ₀ and w at right angles

practice.question: What is the larger eigenvalue of the matrix [[2, 1], [1, 2]]?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Taschner p. 410

labs.title: Cauchy's integral theorem
labs.idea: Integrate a holomorphic function once round a closed curve and you get zero. Only a point where the function is not holomorphic, inside the curve, can change that.

equations.eq: f : G → ℂ holomorphic, G simply connected, Γ closed in G  ⇒  ∮Γ f(z) dz = 0
equations.tex: f: G \to \mathbb{C} \text{ holomorphic}, \; G \text{ simply connected}, \; \Gamma \subset G \text{ closed} \;\Rightarrow\; \oint_\Gamma f(z)\,dz = 0
equations.note: Cauchy's integral theorem (Cauchyscher Integralsatz)
round the pole of 1/z: z = e^(jt), dz = j e^(jt) dt

practice.question: Integrate f(z) = 1/z once round the unit circle, counter-clockwise. What is the imaginary part of the result?
practice.solution: z = e^(jt), dz = j e^(jt) dt, so dz/z = j dt and the integral is j · 2π: imaginary part 2π ≈ 6.283.
